input.rationale: The durable-state experiment for the configuration-recovery question has been executed (receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5): both comparisons are violated with valid witnesses, showing the lost configuration being written into snapshot metadata and surviving a restart with the replay disabled. This batch replaces the account of the question with one that spans all three receipts.

interpretations.rationale: Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off: with the flag on and no snapshot the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: no members at index 0, 268 polls without a leader) although its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself (event 6), and with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter the flag-on node kept the snapshot's index-1 configuration instead of the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11) while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), advancing lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621), so committed configuration entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624) and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is never read back. That state decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and vote admission. First consequence: receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a removed server C from {A,B,C} (event 2: committed configuration at index 5 with two voters), restarted A with the flag on while B was partitioned, and A tracked the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration containing C (event 3); A won the election counting C and committed 'stale-quorum-entry' at index 10 term 4 with apply_error null, its FSM applied it, B's log lacked that index and C's log held it at the same term (event 4). Since A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path, the deciding acknowledgement can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied and reported successful against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration. Second consequence, durable: receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 leaves A in that recovered state on a three-voter cluster (event 6: latest_config_index 0 with no members and committed_config_index 0, against its log's index-1 three-voter entry and staged commit index 4), takes a snapshot through the library's normal path, and reads back metadata recording no configuration at index 0 while the log establishes a three-voter configuration at index 1 (event 7, snapshot_config_matches_log_config false). A then restarts on the same stores with the replay disabled and comes up with an empty configuration at index 0, no leader within 1500ms, in state Follower (event 8). The loss is therefore not confined to the replay path: once written, the snapshot metadata re-imposes it on a restart that never enables the feature. Defect account: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so the node may keep an older or empty membership although its own log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can be permanently unable to participate, can decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match - committing an entry a real voter of that configuration does not hold - and can write the lost configuration into durable snapshot metadata, from which later restarts, including ones with the feature disabled, restore it. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path. The failed first execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution here: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step because the elected leader was not the node being snapshotted, so it produced no comparison result about the target.

knowledge.assertion: The startup configuration scan runs from max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so entries at or below that bound never reach processConfigurationLogEntry at startup.
restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.
Snapshots record the committed configuration and its index that the node currently tracks, and startup restores that metadata into the tracked configuration.

counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) promises only that committed logs are replayed to catch the FSM up and says nothing about membership recovery, so the stale tracked configuration can be read as an unnamed side effect of a feature that never claimed to preserve it. The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the observed consequences are a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain and a durable record that re-imposes the loss.

The commit-rule violation needs the removed server C to stay reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted; if it were stopped or unreachable the same stale configuration would instead leave the node unable to commit. The receipt therefore shows one reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

One could argue the snapshot in the durable-state case is only as good as the state the node tracks, and that a caller should not snapshot a node whose configuration is empty. The counter is that the node is an ordinary cluster member whose own log contains the configuration entries, nothing in the API or the documentation marks its snapshots as unusable, and the resulting metadata then defeats a restart that has the feature disabled, so the corruption outlives the condition that created it.

The flag-off restart's failure to lead could be attributed to the 1500ms observation window rather than to the empty configuration. The counter is the source guard that refuses elections while configurations.latestIndex is zero (raft.go:225-241), together with the sibling controls on the same machinery that elected within about 85ms (receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c, event 6); 1500ms is 30 election timeouts.

The harness assigns roles deliberately (A restarts, B is partitioned, leadership is moved with the library's transfer) and it takes the snapshot explicitly rather than through the automatic cadence. Those choices select the scenario but do not supply the stale or empty configuration, which event 6 shows against the node's own log, nor the acknowledgement, which C's log carries.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469) and is retained as a harness artifact; the later receipts contain the same scenario with both defects exercised.
limitations: All nodes are in-memory transports and stores in one process and the harness uses a test log store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes; the caller-side durability contract of CommitTrackingLogStore is assumed, not verified, and no production store or snapshot store is exercised.

The durable-state case snapshots a node that has no snapshot on its stores and then restarts with the replay disabled; shipping such a snapshot to a follower, or corruption arising from the automatic snapshot cadence, is not exercised, and deleting the corrupt snapshot is not tested as a recovery.

The multi-node case is one prefix shape with one committed removal, keeps the removed server running, and injects no message loss, reordering or crash, so the decision defect is observed under a clean transport.

Schedule variation is limited: the multi-node scenario appears in two receipts with the same operands, the durable-state scenario in one, and the observation windows are 1500ms for non-participation and 2000ms apply timeouts.
interpretations.joint_history: All three receipts are executions of this investigation's fixed experiments on the same captured source revision, in separate workspaces with no shared mutable state. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c established the recovery behaviour on four single-voter prefixes; receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a exercised the same recovery as the setup of a three-voter cluster and observed the commit-rule consequence; receipt c477da09810f4842ba55130320e2a6b5 contains both that three-voter scenario again (events 0-4, with the same operands: a restart tracking the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration against a log whose newest configuration entry is index 4 with two voters, and a commit at index 9 completed with only the removed server's acknowledgement) and the new durable-state scenario (events 5-8, where the same recovery leaves an empty tracked configuration). The repeated scenario reproduces the earlier witness with fresh addresses, so the premises each receipt relies on are observed more than once and the newer receipts only add consequences.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. NewRaft restores the newest usable snapshot, then, only with RestoreCommittedLogs, reads the persisted commit index from the commit-tracking log store, stores it and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754); processLogs sets lastApplied to that index (raft.go:1296-1364). Only after that does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds the node's configuration from the log, and that scan starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the feature off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index, so the scan covers every configuration entry in the log; with the feature on, lastApplied is the commit index, which for a node that committed entries above its newest snapshot is strictly larger, so every configuration entry at an index <= that commit index is skipped even though it is present in the node's log and was applied to the FSM. The skipped entries can only have been processed by processConfigurationLogEntry, the sole writer of the tracked configuration state, and its startup caller is exactly that scan; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The resulting configuration state is not inert: configurations.latestIndex == 0 makes a follower refuse to start an election (raft.go:225-241), and configurations.latest supplies quorumSize, the voter set counted by checkLeaderLease, the membership map used by the leader's commitment, and the inConfiguration/hasVote admission checks for vote grants (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Two consequences follow directly: a node with no snapshot recovers an empty configuration and can never elect itself (no reachable producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists in a single-voter cluster), and a node with a snapshot recovers the snapshot's older membership, including a member set that omits an entry its log already committed. The existing test for this feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration is identical to the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this case. The defect is scoped to deployments that enable RestoreCommittedLogs and use a commit-tracking log store; the intended duty is that the node recover the configuration its own log establishes, which the scan exists to do.
counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) describes replaying committed logs to bring the FSM up to date and says nothing about configuration recovery, so one could argue that a stale configuration view is an unnamed side effect rather than a broken contract. The counter is that the scan at api.go:610-621 exists precisely to rebuild configuration state from the log at startup, and its start index is the only reason entries are skipped; no other path restores that state after the replay.

The skip also removes work: with RestoreCommittedLogs, configuration entries below the persisted commit index were already delivered to the FSM as commit tuples, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has seen them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is not derived from the FSM.
limitations: The predicate recorded here is source-derived; the fixed experiment for this question has been submitted with this batch and its retained receipt is not yet part of this account. A native local run of the same harness was used only to validate operands while constructing it and is not offered as evidence.

Both prefix cases restart a single-voter cluster on an in-memory transport with an in-memory commit-tracking log store, so the observation window (1.5s = 30 election timeouts) measures non-participation of that node, not of a multi-node cluster.

The stale-membership consequence for a leader's commit index is argued from the code path that builds the commitment from configurations.latest; no scenario in this batch partitions a multi-node cluster to show a commit decided by a member set that the committed configuration does not contain.

The persisted commit index is staged only on log writes (raft.go:1392-1405, 1553-1561), so its value in the stored prefix is not necessarily the highest committed index; this does not affect the ordering argument, since any staged value above 0 exceeds the snapshot index in these cases.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes (bootstrap, election through the normal path, client applies, shutdown) on top of their retained log, stable and snapshot stores, twice per prefix shape, with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off, and observed each restarted node for 1500ms (30 election/heartbeat timeouts at 50ms, polled every 5ms). Comparison 0 (flag on, no snapshot) is violated by witness event 2: the node ended in state Follower, leader_observed false over 268 polls, with latest_config_index 0, latest_config_ids empty and latest_config_voters 0, while the same prefix's log holds LogConfiguration@1 with one voter (event 0) and the persisted commit index was 5 (event 1). Comparison 1 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 6: leader_observed true, latest_config_index 1 and latest_config_ids equal to the log's entry. Comparison 2 (flag on) is violated by witness event 3: recovered configuration index 0 with no servers against log_last_config_index 1 and log_last_config_ids carrying the single voter. Comparison 3 (flag off) holds at event 7 with config_matches_last_log_config true. Comparison 4 (flag on, snapshot at index 6 followed by a committed AddNonvoter at index 7) is violated by witness event 11: recovered latest_config_index 1 with exactly one voter and zero nonvoters (the snapshot's committed configuration, snapshot_index 6 in event 8), while the node's own log's newest configuration entry is index 7 with voters 1 and nonvoters 1 including the added peer. Comparison 5 (flag off, same prefix shape) holds at event 15 with the recovered configuration at index 7 including that peer. The controls differ from the violations only in the flag, on prefixes built the same way, so the difference tracks the replay path and not the prefix shape. Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs reads the persisted commit index, stores it and calls processLogs, which advances lastApplied to it (api.go:723-754), and only afterwards does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state, starting at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the flag off lastApplied is the snapshot index and the scan covers the log; with the flag on it is the commit index, so committed configuration entries at or below it are never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry, the only writer of r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The consequence recorded here is that the restarted node's decision state can be the snapshot's configuration or an empty one: with latest_config_index 0 the follower branch refuses to start an election (raft.go:225-241), which is terminal for the no-snapshot case because no reachable peer can ever send a configuration entry, and the stale view is what quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership and the vote-admission checks consume (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). The duty is not documented as waived: the flag's doc comment speaks only about catching up the FSM (config.go:243-254) and says nothing about membership, while the startup scan exists precisely to rebuild that state from the log. The existing test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-0.explanation: At startup only two inputs write the tracked configuration state, in this order: restoreSnapshot copies the snapshot's committed configuration and its index into both committed and latest (api.go:645-684), and the scan at api.go:610-621 replays processConfigurationLogEntry over log indices from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 upward. The restored FSM is not a source: the ConfigurationStore interface is write-only from raft's perspective (fsm.go:110-119 invokes StoreConfiguration; nothing reads it back), so the log scan is the only input that can roll the tracked configuration forward through the log. This is corroborated by the retained receipt: in the two feature-on cases the recovered configuration was exactly the snapshot's committed configuration (event 11: index 1, one voter, no nonvoters) or the empty configuration (events 2 and 3: index 0, no servers), never the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index 1 in the no-snapshot case per event 0, index 7 in the snapshot case per event 8).

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Partially answered. The receipt shows one decision that the stale view changed outside the node: in the snapshot case with the flag on, the node reached leadership (event 10: final_state Leader, leader_observed true, commit_index and last_applied 10) while its tracked configuration was the snapshot's index-1 configuration with one voter and no nonvoters, not its log's committed index-7 configuration (event 11). That election was nevertheless still justifiable under the real committed configuration, because the omitted member was a nonvoter and the voting majority of both member sets is the local node, so the observed election is not yet a quorum formed from members the committed configuration excludes. A commit index advanced by a stale voter set, for example after a committed removal or a committed demotion, remains open and is not established by this receipt.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks from lastApplied+1 to that index, accumulating commit tuples and flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries, delivering each batch through a select that waits for r.fsmMutateCh or r.shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312, 1336-1350). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and is consumed only by runFSM, which NewRaft starts after the replay returns (api.go:636-638). At startup lastApplied is the restored snapshot index, so the replay spans the committed log above the snapshot, and the number of sends is ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries). With the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 128 sends at 8192 entries, so any restart whose committed range above the snapshot exceeds 8192 entries blocks inside NewRaft on the 129th send, with the FSM goroutine not yet started, no timeout, and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller has not received the Raft object. The trigger is a legal configuration or workload: a smaller positive MaxAppendEntries lowers the bound proportionally, and a node that has never snapshotted (or whose snapshots lag its write rate) exceeds the default bound without any tuning. The failure is a startup liveness failure, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group loses one member permanently. No repair is enabled in the blocked state: the only escape from the send is a shutdown channel that only a caller holding the returned object could close.
counterevidence: The default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound rather than far above it, so on a fully auto-snapshotting node the block needs the range to overshoot the bound, for example because more entries were appended between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completion. The claim does not rest on the default configuration alone: SnapshotThreshold and MaxAppendEntries are both legal config fields, and a store that keeps its log without snapshots reaches any range.

The existing feature test (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a log of about a hundred entries, far below the bound, so its passing result is not counterevidence to a bound that begins around 8192 default entries.
limitations: The receipt for this question's fixed experiment is not yet part of this account; a native local run of the same harness was used only to validate the operands during construction and is not offered as evidence.

The harness restarts a single-voter in-memory cluster with SnapshotThreshold raised so that no automatic snapshot is taken; it does not exercise a lowered MaxAppendEntries, an overshooting auto-snapshot, or a multi-node member loss.

The blocked state is reported as non-return within a fixed window plus a stack sample of the blocked goroutine; the permanence argument comes from the source, since nothing consumes the channel before runFSM starts.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarted two independently built single-voter prefixes whose retained store holds a committed log about 9000 entries above an absent snapshot: event 16 records 9000 applied commands, log_last_index 9002, staged_commit_index 9001, snapshot_index 0 and the resulting 141 replay batches at MaxAppendEntries 64, and event 19 records the same for the control prefix. Comparison 0 is violated by witness event 18: the restart admitted by event 17 (restore_committed_logs true) did not return from NewRaft within the 8000ms window (new_raft_returned false), and the sampled goroutine stack names the replay frames in order, processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, which is the batch send on fsmMutateCh. Comparison 1 holds at event 21: the same prefix shape restarted with the flag off (admission event 20) returned from NewRaft in 1ms (new_raft_returned true, elapsed_ms 1) and then reached leadership (event 22, final_state Leader, commit_index 9003). The two restarts differ only in the flag, so the non-return is not a property of the prefix, the log volume or the transport. Source side, the mechanism is settled and makes the block permanent rather than slow: processLogs delivers each batch of at most MaxAppendEntries commit tuples through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after restoreFromCommittedLogs has returned. The replay needs ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) = ceil(9001/64) = 141 sends, so the 129th send waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the call it is blocking has finished, with no timeout, and the only escape is a shutdown channel that the caller cannot close because NewRaft has not returned the object. Scope of the defect statement: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays needs more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; the bound is 8192 entries with the default MaxAppendEntries of 64, and is smaller in proportion to any smaller legal value. The failure is startup liveness, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating at all, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group permanently loses one member. The counterevidence is about how easily a default deployment reaches the bound, not about whether the block occurs once it is reached.

knowledge.assertion: Each batch is delivered with a select between a send on fsmMutateCh and shutdownCh, so a full channel with no consumer waits indefinitely.
fsmMutateCh has capacity 128 and its consumer runFSM starts only after the startup replay returns.
The number of entries replayed above the snapshot is what sets the batch count, and the automatic snapshot cadence is the only bound on that range in a default deployment.
With the flag on, lastApplied is set to the persisted commit index before the replay, so the replay range spans the committed log above the snapshot.

counterevidence: The evidence that NewRaft did not return is a single 8000ms window plus one stack sample (event 18). The claim that the wait is permanent does not rest on that sample: the source shows no timeout, exactly one consumer started after the blocked call returns, and an escape that requires an object the caller has not received. The flag-off control returning in 1ms (event 21) shows the wait is not simply the cost of the work.

With the default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 and MaxAppendEntries of 64, the automatic snapshot cadence keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound, so a default node blocks only when the range overshoots the bound, for example because entries kept arriving between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completing. The harness therefore raised SnapshotThreshold, a legal Config field, to place the range unambiguously above the bound. The receipt establishes that crossing the bound blocks startup; it does not measure how often a default deployment crosses it.

The control's FSM catch-up was not observed to completion: event 22 samples last_applied 0 right after leadership, so the receipt shows only that the flag-off restart returns promptly and elects itself, not that its later catch-up finishes.

The blocked goroutine was abandoned inside the test process; the test completed because NewRaft ran in a separate goroutine. That is a harness choice, not a repair: the abandoned call still cannot be shut down, since the caller never received the object.
limitations: Both prefixes are single-voter in-memory clusters over an in-memory commit-tracking log store with SnapshotThreshold raised so no automatic snapshot moves the replay bound; the proportional relation for smaller MaxAppendEntries is source-derived (ceil(range/MaxAppendEntries) against a 128-slot buffer) and was not measured.
No multi-node cluster is exercised, so the member loss caused by a node that cannot start is argued rather than observed.
The bound itself depends on the caller-side store: the replay range comes from the store's persisted commit index, and the harness uses a test store whose staging is not atomic with its log writes.
Only one wait length (8000ms) was used, and the same case was not repeated; schedule variation is not characterized.

interpretations.rationale: Two executions of the same fixed experiment agree. Receipt e82594cc274340f0a961608cda519e00 first reruns the original pair: event 16 records a prefix with 9000 applied commands, log_last_index 9002, staged_commit_index 9001, snapshot_index 0 and 141 replay batches at MaxAppendEntries 64; the flag-on restart admitted by event 17 did not return from NewRaft within 8000ms (event 18, new_raft_returned false) and the sampled stack again names processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, while the flag-off restart of the same shape returned in 5ms (event 21) and became leader (event 22). Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f recorded the same outcome with return in 1ms, so the block reproduces across two independent executions with different addresses. The revision then measures the bound: events 23 and 27 record two prefixes built the same way at MaxAppendEntries 16 with 1501 and 3001 replayed entries, that is 94 and 188 batches; the below-bound restart (comparison 0, event 25) returned from NewRaft in 0ms, and the above-bound restart (comparison 1, witness event 29) did not return, with the stack sample naming the same replay frames. Because the two cases share the flag, the batch size, the store machinery and the harness, and differ only in replay volume, the boundary between them measures the completion bound as 128 batches times MaxAppendEntries (2048 entries at 16, 8192 at the default 64) rather than a fixed amount of log. Source side, the mechanism is settled and makes the wait permanent rather than slow: processLogs delivers each batch through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after the replay returns; the replay needs ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) sends, so once the count passes 128 the 129th send waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the blocked call finishes, with no timeout and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller never receives the object. Defect statement, now scoped to the measured bound: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays exceeds 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; at the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 8192 entries, and it is proportionally smaller for any smaller legal value, as measured at 16. The failure is startup liveness, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group permanently loses one member.

interpretations.rationale: Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off. With the flag on and no snapshot, the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: latest_config_index 0, no members, 268 polls with no leader) even though its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), while the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself in 17 polls (event 6); with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter, the flag-on node recovered the snapshot's index-1 configuration and never the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11), while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), which advances lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621); committed configuration entries at or below that bound are therefore never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624), and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is not read back. The tracked configuration is what decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and the vote-admission checks. Consequence, now observed. Receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a builds three voters A, B and C (event 0), snapshots A while the committed configuration is still {A,B,C} (event 1, snapshot index 4), removes C so the committed configuration becomes {A,B} at log index 5 (event 2), then restarts A with the flag on while B is partitioned and C stays connected. A's tracked configuration is the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration and it contains C (event 3: latest_config_index 1, latest_config_voters 3, latest_config_ids including C, log_config_index 5, log_config_voters 2). A then won the election - counting C's vote, a server the committed configuration no longer contains - and, in event 4, applied the client command 'stale-quorum-entry' with apply_error null at index 10 term 4, advancing its commit index and applied index to 10, while B's log does not contain that index and C's log contains it at the same term 4. A's own match index alone cannot form a majority of three, and B had no transport path to A, so the second match the commitment counted can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied to A's FSM and reported successful to the client by a quorum that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}. Defect account for the whole question: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership although its log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can then be permanently unable to participate (empty configuration), or, as observed here, decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match, committing an entry that a real voter of the committed configuration does not hold. The failed predecessor execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution of this interpretation: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step with 'nothing new to snapshot' because the elected leader was not A and A had applied no entry, so it produced no comparison result about the target. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Resolved by receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a. The stale recovered configuration changed two decisions observable outside the node: the election A won (event 4, a_became_leader true) counted C, a server the committed configuration had removed, towards the majority of its tracked three-voter configuration, and the commit that followed (event 4: entry index 10, term 4, apply_error null, a_commit_index 10, a_applied_index 10, a_fsm_applied_payload true) was decided while the committed configuration's other voter B, partitioned from A, did not hold the entry (b_log_has_entry false) and the removed server C did (c_log_has_entry true, c_entry_term 4). Because A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path to A, the second match must have come from C, so the commit rule was applied against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace. NewRaft restores the newest usable snapshot, then, only with RestoreCommittedLogs, reads the persisted commit index from the commit-tracking log store, stores it and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754); processLogs sets lastApplied to that index (raft.go:1296-1364). Only after that does NewRaft run the scan that rebuilds the node's configuration from the log, and that scan starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) + 1 (api.go:602-621). With the feature off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index, so the scan covers every configuration entry in the log; with the feature on, lastApplied is the commit index, which for a node that committed entries above its newest snapshot is strictly larger, so every configuration entry at an index <= that commit index is skipped even though it is present in the node's log and was applied to the FSM. The skipped entries can only have been processed by processConfigurationLogEntry, the sole writer of the tracked configuration state, and its startup caller is exactly that scan; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into r.configurations (raft.go:1605-1624). The resulting configuration state is not inert: configurations.latestIndex == 0 makes a follower refuse to start an election (raft.go:225-241), and configurations.latest supplies quorumSize, the voter set counted by checkLeaderLease, the membership map used by the leader's commitment, and the inConfiguration/hasVote admission checks for vote grants (raft.go:456-467, 1085-1094; commitment.go:35-64). Two consequences follow directly: a node with no snapshot recovers an empty configuration and can never elect itself (no reachable producer of AppendEntries or configuration entries exists in a single-voter cluster), and a node with a snapshot recovers the snapshot's older membership, including a member set that omits an entry its log already committed. The existing test for this feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration is identical to the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this case. The defect is scoped to deployments that enable RestoreCommittedLogs and use a commit-tracking log store; the intended duty is that the node recover the configuration its own log establishes, which the scan exists to do.
counterevidence: The doc comment for RestoreCommittedLogs (config.go:243-254) describes replaying committed logs to bring the FSM up to date and says nothing about configuration recovery, so one could argue that a stale configuration view is an unnamed side effect rather than a broken contract. The counter is that the scan at api.go:610-621 exists precisely to rebuild configuration state from the log at startup, and its start index is the only reason entries are skipped; no other path restores that state after the replay.

The skip also removes work: with RestoreCommittedLogs, configuration entries below the persisted commit index were already delivered to the FSM as commit tuples, so an FSM implementing ConfigurationStore has seen them. That does not restore r.configurations, which is raft's own decision input and is not derived from the FSM.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-0.explanation: At startup only two inputs write the tracked configuration state, in this order: restoreSnapshot copies the snapshot's committed configuration and its index into both committed and latest (api.go:645-684), and the scan at api.go:610-621 replays processConfigurationLogEntry over log indices from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 upward. The restored FSM is not a source: the ConfigurationStore interface is write-only from raft's perspective (fsm.go:110-119 invokes StoreConfiguration; nothing reads it back), so the log scan is the only input that can roll the tracked configuration forward through the log. This is corroborated by the retained receipt: in the two feature-on cases the recovered configuration was exactly the snapshot's committed configuration (event 11: index 1, one voter, no nonvoters) or the empty configuration (events 2 and 3: index 0, no servers), never the newest configuration entry in the node's own log (index 1 in the no-snapshot case per event 0, index 7 in the snapshot case per event 8).

The receipt shows one decision that the stale view changed outside the node: in the snapshot case with the flag on, the node reached leadership (event 10: final_state Leader, leader_observed true, commit_index and last_applied 10) while its tracked configuration was the snapshot's index-1 configuration with one voter and no nonvoters, not its log's committed index-7 configuration (event 11). interpretations.rationale: Source trace. With Config.RestoreCommittedLogs set, NewRaft reads the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754). processLogs walks from lastApplied+1 to that index, accumulating commit tuples and flushing a batch whenever the batch reaches config.MaxAppendEntries, delivering each batch through a select that waits for r.fsmMutateCh or r.shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312, 1336-1350). fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560) and is consumed only by runFSM, which NewRaft starts after the replay returns (api.go:636-638). At startup lastApplied is the restored snapshot index, so the replay spans the committed log above the snapshot, and the number of sends is ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries). With the default MaxAppendEntries of 64 that is 128 sends at 8192 entries, so any restart whose committed range above the snapshot exceeds 8192 entries blocks inside NewRaft on the 129th send, with the FSM goroutine not yet started, no timeout, and no reachable way to close shutdownCh because the caller has not received the Raft object. The trigger is a legal configuration or workload: a smaller positive MaxAppendEntries lowers the bound proportionally, and a node that has never snapshotted (or whose snapshots lag its write rate) exceeds the default bound without any tuning. The failure is a startup liveness failure, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group loses one member permanently. No repair is enabled in the blocked state: the only escape from the send is a shutdown channel that only a caller holding the returned object could close.
counterevidence: The default SnapshotThreshold of 8192 keeps the replay range near the 8192-entry bound rather than far above it, so on a fully auto-snapshotting node the block needs the range to overshoot the bound, for example because more entries were appended between the snapshot trigger and the snapshot completion. The claim does not rest on the default configuration alone: SnapshotThreshold and MaxAppendEntries are both legal config fields, and a store that keeps its log without snapshots reaches any range.

The existing feature test (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a log of about a hundred entries, far below the bound, so its passing result is not counterevidence to a bound that begins around 8192 default entries.
limitations: The receipt for this question's fixed experiment is not yet part of this account; a native local run of the same harness was used only to validate the operands during construction and is not offered as evidence.

The harness restarts a single-voter in-memory cluster with SnapshotThreshold raised so that no automatic snapshot is taken; it does not exercise a lowered MaxAppendEntries, an overshooting auto-snapshot, or a multi-node member loss.

The blocked state is reported as non-return within a fixed window plus a stack sample of the blocked goroutine; the permanence argument comes from the source, since nothing consumes the channel before runFSM starts.

interpretations.rationale: Receipt 3d04552f58e548b0ae089192392b564f restarted two independently built single-voter prefixes whose retained store holds a committed log about 9000 entries above an absent snapshot: event 16 records 9000 applied commands, log_last_index 9002, staged_commit_index 9001, snapshot_index 0 and the resulting 141 replay batches at MaxAppendEntries 64, and event 19 records the same for the control prefix. Comparison 0 is violated by witness event 18: the restart admitted by event 17 (restore_committed_logs true) did not return from NewRaft within the 8000ms window (new_raft_returned false), and the sampled goroutine stack names the replay frames in order, processLogs at raft.go:1346 called from restoreFromCommittedLogs at api.go:753 called from NewRaft, which is the batch send on fsmMutateCh. Comparison 1 holds at event 21: the same prefix shape restarted with the flag off (admission event 20) returned from NewRaft in 1ms (new_raft_returned true, elapsed_ms 1) and then reached leadership (event 22, final_state Leader, commit_index 9003). The two restarts differ only in the flag, so the non-return is not a property of the prefix, the log volume or the transport. Source side, the mechanism is settled and makes the block permanent rather than slow: processLogs delivers each batch of at most MaxAppendEntries commit tuples through a select whose only other case is shutdownCh (raft.go:1302-1312), fsmMutateCh is created with capacity 128 (api.go:560), and its only consumer runFSM is started by api.go:636-638 after restoreFromCommittedLogs has returned. The replay needs ceil((commitIndex - lastApplied)/MaxAppendEntries) = ceil(9001/64) = 141 sends, so the 129th send waits for a consumer that cannot exist until the call it is blocking has finished, with no timeout, and the only escape is a shutdown channel that the caller cannot close because NewRaft has not returned the object. Scope of the defect statement: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft cannot complete startup whenever the committed log it replays needs more than 128 batches, that is more than 128*MaxAppendEntries entries above the restored snapshot index; the bound is 8192 entries with the default MaxAppendEntries of 64, and is smaller in proportion to any smaller legal value. The failure is startup liveness, not a wrong decision: the node never begins participating at all, so a single-voter group stays down and a larger group permanently loses one member. The counterevidence is about how easily a default deployment reaches the bound, not about whether the block occurs once it is reached.

interpretations.rationale: Recovery. Receipt 9a373c13725a42aa9f48f59c0f2f2f1c restarted four real single-voter prefixes on their retained stores with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs on and off. With the flag on and no snapshot, the node recovered an empty configuration (event 2: latest_config_index 0, no members, 268 polls with no leader) even though its log holds the bootstrap configuration entry at index 1 (event 0), while the flag-off control on the same prefix shape tracked that entry and elected itself in 17 polls (event 6); with a snapshot taken before a committed AddNonvoter, the flag-on node recovered the snapshot's index-1 configuration and never the log's committed index-7 configuration (events 10, 11), while the flag-off control recovered index 7 (event 15). Source side, the mechanism is settled: restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the persisted commit index and calls processLogs with it (api.go:723-754), which advances lastApplied before NewRaft runs the scan that rebuilds tracked configuration state from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 (api.go:602-621); committed configuration entries at or below that bound are therefore never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go:1605-1624), and the FSM's ConfigurationStore is not read back. The tracked configuration is what decides election eligibility (raft.go:225-246), quorum size (raft.go:1085-1094), the leader's commitment membership (raft.go:456-467, commitment.go:35-64) and the vote-admission checks. Consequence, now observed. Receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a builds three voters A, B and C (event 0), snapshots A while the committed configuration is still {A,B,C} (event 1, snapshot index 4), removes C so the committed configuration becomes {A,B} at log index 5 (event 2), then restarts A with the flag on while B is partitioned and C stays connected. A's tracked configuration is the snapshot's index-1 three-voter configuration and it contains C (event 3: latest_config_index 1, latest_config_voters 3, latest_config_ids including C, log_config_index 5, log_config_voters 2). A then won the election - counting C's vote, a server the committed configuration no longer contains - and, in event 4, applied the client command 'stale-quorum-entry' with apply_error null at index 10 term 4, advancing its commit index and applied index to 10, while B's log does not contain that index and C's log contains it at the same term 4. A's own match index alone cannot form a majority of three, and B had no transport path to A, so the second match the commitment counted can only have come from C: the entry was committed, applied to A's FSM and reported successful to the client by a quorum that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}. Defect account for the whole question: with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and a commit-tracking log store, NewRaft cannot roll the node's tracked membership configuration forward past max(snapshot index, persisted commit index), so a restarted node may keep an older or empty membership although its log already contains the committed configuration entries; the recovered node can then be permanently unable to participate (empty configuration), or, as observed here, decide leadership and commit index from a member set the committed configuration does not match, committing an entry that a real voter of the committed configuration does not hold. The failed predecessor execution of the multi-node experiment (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1) is retained in the run's logs but is not cited as an execution of this interpretation: it stopped in the harness at the snapshot step with 'nothing new to snapshot' because the elected leader was not A and A had applied no entry, so it produced no comparison result about the target. The library's own test for the feature (raft_test.go:1183-1270) restarts with a snapshot whose configuration already equals the final configuration and asserts only the applied index, so it does not constrain this path.

98ee8dfd5fac4b84915f91ed4b094bcf-gap-1.explanation: Resolved by receipt 79a9cc34b3ce42e197c384775efecc3a. The stale recovered configuration changed two decisions observable outside the node: the election A won (event 4, a_became_leader true) counted C, a server the committed configuration had removed, towards the majority of its tracked three-voter configuration, and the commit that followed (event 4: entry index 10, term 4, apply_error null, a_commit_index 10, a_applied_index 10, a_fsm_applied_payload true) was decided while the committed configuration's other voter B, partitioned from A, did not hold the entry (b_log_has_entry false) and the removed server C did (c_log_has_entry true, c_entry_term 4). Because A's own match cannot form a majority of three and B had no transport path to A, the second match must have come from C, so the commit rule was applied against a member set that is not a majority of the committed configuration {A,B}.

restoreFromCommittedLogs stores the store's commit index and calls processLogs with it only when the flag is set, which advances lastApplied to that index before the scan runs.
processConfigurationLogEntry is the only writer of the tracked configuration state; FSM-side configuration storage does not feed back into it.
The tracked latest configuration feeds quorumSize, the leader's commitment membership, leader-lease voter counting and the vote-admission checks.
A follower with configurations.latestIndex equal to 0 does not start an election, which is terminal when no reachable peer can supply a configuration entry.

The counter is that the startup scan at api.go:610-621 exists to rebuild that state from the log, and the replay merely moves its lower bound; the observed consequence is a commit decided against a member set the committed configuration does not contain.

The violating scenario needs the removed server C to stay running and reachable after its removal, since its acknowledgement is what the stale majority counted. If an operator removes a server and also stops it, or if it is unreachable, the same stale configuration would instead leave A unable to commit, so the receipt shows the reachable-removed-server case rather than every case.

The harness chose A as the restarting leader and B as the partitioned node, and it moved leadership to A with the library's leadership transfer before the snapshot; those are setup choices. They do not supply the stale configuration (event 3 shows A tracking a configuration its log had already superseded) and they do not supply the acknowledgement (C's log holds the entry at the same term), but a different assignment of roles is not exercised.

The receipt shows that the leader committed and applied the entry and returned success to the caller, and that the committed configuration's other voter lacked it; it does not follow the entry to a later term to observe an actual loss from a state machine, so the demonstrated violation is of the commitment rule rather than a completed divergence.

The first execution of the multi-node experiment failed in the harness before any comparison (receipt 4ed46b198c8d41618cc855df0a63d469, exit 1, 'snapshot on A failed: nothing new to snapshot'), and its single parsed event carries no configuration operands; it is retained as a harness artifact and not as evidence about the target.
